deep.reconstruction:
Context: this is the draft of Riemann's answer to the Paris Academy prize question on heat conduction (the 'Commentatio mathematica, qua respondere tentatur quaestioni ab Ill^ma Academia Parisiensi propositae', 1861). The previous page set up the anisotropic heat equation (I): sum_i d/dx_i ( sum_i' a_{i i'} du/dx_i' ) = h du/dt, with a symmetric and positive definite and h the heat capacity per unit volume. On this page Riemann changes the independent variables to arbitrary curvilinear coordinates s_1, s_2, s_3.

Step 1 (variational characterization). Riemann asserts that (I) is necessary and sufficient for the following: for every infinitesimal variation delta u, the quantity
(A) delta ∫∫∫ sum a_{i i'} u_{x_i} u_{x_i'} dx + ∫∫∫ 2h u_t delta u dx
depends only on the values of delta u on the boundary surface. Only u is varied; u_t is held fixed.
Implicit step (mine): by symmetry of a the variation of the first integral is ∫ 2 (a grad u)·grad(delta u) dx. Integrating by parts gives a boundary term minus ∫ 2[div(a grad u) - h u_t] delta u dx. So (A) reduces to a boundary term for all delta u iff div(a grad u) = h u_t, which is (I).

Step 2 (change of variables). Put P = (ds_mu/dx_i) and J = det P, written by Riemann in Jacobi's notation Σ± ds_1/dx_1 ds_2/dx_2 ds_3/dx_3. Then u_{x_i} = sum_mu u_{s_mu} ds_mu/dx_i and dx = ds/J. Hence (A) becomes
(B) delta ∫∫∫ sum b_{mu nu} u_{s_mu} u_{s_nu} ds + ∫∫∫ 2k u_t delta u ds,
where b_{mu nu} = (1/J) sum a_{i i'} (ds_mu/dx_i)(ds_nu/dx_i') and k = h/J. In matrix form b = P a P^T / J.
Because the boundary-only property is coordinate-invariant, the transformed equation is sum_mu d/ds_mu( sum_nu b_{mu nu} u_{s_nu} ) = k u_t. This conclusion is implicit (mine), but it is the evident point of the argument. A crossed-out first attempt at the definition of b precedes the final one.

Step 3 (determinants and adjugates). Let A = det a and B = det b. Let alpha and beta be the adjoint (adjugate) forms of a and b. Riemann writes the ternary forms in Gauss's notation (a11,a22,a33 / a23,a31,a12). He states:
- A = B·J. Check: det b = J^{-3} J^2 A = A/J.
- beta_{mu nu} = sum alpha_{i i'} (dx_i/ds_mu)(dx_i'/ds_nu), i.e. adj b = Q^T (adj a) Q with Q = P^{-1} = (dx/ds). Check: adj b = B b^{-1} = (A/J) · J P^{-T} a^{-1} P^{-1} = P^{-T} (A a^{-1}) P^{-1}.
- Hence sum alpha_{i i'} dx_i dx_i' = sum beta_{mu nu} ds_mu ds_nu, since dx = Q ds. In other words, the adjugate of the conductivity form transforms as a covariant quadratic differential form (a metric).
- h/A = k/B, since k = h/J and B = A/J. So the scalar h/A is invariant.

Conclusion: transforming equation (I) reduces to transforming the quadratic differential expression sum alpha_{i i'} dx_i dx_i', together with the invariant h/A. The next page uses this to reduce the problem 'can u depend on only two of the variables s' to the question whether a given ternary differential form can be transformed into another. Riemann says this will be treated by Gauss's method from the theory of curved surfaces, which is the germ of the curvature-tensor criterion of the Commentatio.
errors: No mathematical errors. All three stated relations (A = B J, the transformation law for beta, h/A = k/B) are correct.
Implicit assumption: J > 0 (orientation preserved). Otherwise k and b would change sign and lose positivity; Riemann does not state this.

The variational formulation is slightly non-standard: delta acts only on the gradient integral while u_t is held fixed. This is legitimate as a statement about the Euler–Lagrange expression, but it is not a true variational principle for the parabolic equation. It is used correctly here.
The derivation of the transformed PDE from (B) is left implicit.

results.what: Characterization of the divergence-form heat equation via the first variation of the Dirichlet-type energy ∫ a grad u·grad u plus a source term 2h u_t delta u (boundary-only dependence)
results.modern_name: Weak/variational (Euler–Lagrange) form of an elliptic divergence-form operator; coordinate invariance via Dirichlet integral
results.usually_credited_to: Euler–Lagrange, Green, Dirichlet, Jacobi (transformation of Laplacian via variational principle, 1830s)

results.what: Transformation of the conductivity tensor under change of variables: b = P a P^T / det P, k = h/det P
results.modern_name: Transformation law of a contravariant tensor density (weight 1)
results.usually_credited_to: Jacobi / Lamé (curvilinear coordinates); tensor formulation Christoffel, Ricci

results.what: The adjugate of the conductivity form, sum alpha dx dx, is an invariant quadratic differential form (covariant metric), with h/A invariant; transforming the heat equation reduces to the equivalence problem for this form
results.modern_name: Inverse conductivity tensor as a Riemannian metric (anisotropic conduction ↔ Laplace–Beltrami on (M,g)); equivalence problem for quadratic differential forms
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann, Paris Commentatio 1861 (published in Werke 1876); equivalence problem later by Christoffel and Lipschitz (1869)

deep.surprise_reason: This page is a draft of the opening of Riemann's 1861 Paris Commentatio, published in his Collected Works (1876). The reduction of the heat equation to the transformation of sum alpha dx dx is a well-known and well-credited part of that work. The draft adds only minor variants, such as the crossed-out first definition of b.

The crossed-out line before the definition of b_{mu,nu} is an abandoned first attempt: a fragment like 'Σ a_{i,i'} ds_mu/dx_i dx_nu/dx_i' ... ∂x_i' with a stray 'dx' above. It is not mathematically meaningful as transcribed.
Σ± ds_1/dx_1 ds_2/dx_2 ds_3/dx_3 denotes the Jacobian determinant (Jacobi's notation); the transcription's rendering is correct.
